name: Requirements
one_liner: Features and stories, each with a business or enabler perspective, prioritised in one list.
purpose: Requirements describe the product or service features needed to satisfy stakeholders' needs. When requirements are not entirely known, or the rate of change is high, agile and Lean UX approaches yield better results than fixing them upfront. To manage them, PM²-Agile uses two dimensions: the Abstraction Level, expressed through Features and Stories, and the Implementation Perspective, expressed through Business and Enabler items.
meta: Abstraction Level (features, stories) and Implementation Perspective (business, enabler)

items: Feature — a proposed service addressing business, customer and user needs
Features are described in the Project Charter with a high level of abstraction
Features (functional units) are decomposed into stories (working units) to fit an iteration
Story — a small, vertical slice of system behaviour supporting incremental development
Stories are referred to as Work Units or Work Items and collected in a prioritised Work Items List
Business Feature — a feature with a business perspective
Enabler Feature — a feature with an enablement perspective
User Story — a story with a business perspective
Enabler Story — a story with an enablement perspective
Enablement Work covers architecture, infrastructure, evaluating options, legal compliance, continuous improvement, other non-functional requirements

diagram.sec: The reporting units these map onto
items: Delivery units — work packages, deliveries
Functional units — features
Work units — user stories, enabler stories, bugs

diagram.sec: Three strategic risks in identifying requirements
items: Requirements derived from a known solution express the 'how' rather than the 'what'
Requirements are investment items and may duplicate capabilities that already exist
Without clarifying the problem first, opportunities are missed and enterprise impact underestimated
Combine Business Value with the 'Size' of a feature
Highest business value with the shortest turn-around time is delivered first
In higher-risk projects, weigh the risk reduction factor — higher risk, higher priority
Involve the Business Manager, the Project Owner and the Business Implementation Group

fields.what: A description of product or service features that are required to satisfy the stakeholders' needs.
fields.pollux: 'Exposure by member state, instrument and maturity, traceable to the platform.'

fields.what: If both requestor and provider are certain the specification describes the solution completely, the traditional upfront planning approach can be used.
fields.pollux: True on CASTOR, which replaced a system that already did a defined job.

fields.what: When requirements are not entirely known or the rate of change is high, agile and Lean UX approaches yield better results.
fields.pollux: Each quarter the reporting requirements change — so POLLUX went agile.

fields.what: Good agile organisation creates conditions for requestor and provider co-evolution through regular exposure to their agreements' interpretation.
fields.pollux: Curie and the team reinterpret the report definition every fortnight.

fields.what: Requirements derived from knowledge of possible solutions express the how rather than the what, limiting discovery of the best solution.
fields.pollux: 'Rebuild the spreadsheets in a portal' would have fixed the wrong solution.

fields.what: Each requirement is an investment item and a recurring expense, and may duplicate capabilities that already exist and could be reused.
fields.pollux: Einstein checks what the CASTOR platform already provides before building.

fields.what: The problem or need must be fully documented in the PM² Business Case before gathering requirements, then implementation impact evaluated.
fields.who: BM responsible for the Business Case
fields.pollux: The Business Case documents the five-day, four-analyst quarter-end problem.

fields.what: PM²-Agile acknowledges the key role of Features and Stories in describing the solution's behaviour at different abstraction levels.
fields.pollux: 'Reconciliation panel' as feature; its stories as the work items.

fields.what: The perspective cannot be restricted to business: the underlying work supporting the business features is the role of Business and Enabler items.
fields.pollux: Traceability plumbing is enabler work; the exposure view is business work.

fields.what: A proposed service, within the context of a solution, that exists to address the needs of the business, the customer and the user.
fields.pollux: The charter approved 12 Oct 2028 lists the portal's features.

fields.what: Features are described with a high level of abstraction so all layers understand the scope, with context and a benefit hypothesis to verify on delivery.
fields.pollux: Each feature carries the benefit hypothesis behind criteria SC1 to SC5.

fields.what: Features must be prioritised to execute the release strategy, involving key stakeholders such as the BM, the Project Owner and the BIG.
fields.pollux: Hopper and Nightingale weigh in on which views come first.

fields.what: Combine business value and feature size; the highest value with the shortest turn-around is delivered first, weighing risk reduction where relevant.
fields.pollux: Read-only exposure by member state is the fastest valuable slice for Release 1.

fields.what: A feature is developed and delivered in the context of a release across several iterations, so it must be decomposed into stories.
fields.pollux: The reconciliation panel spans several two-week iterations before Release 2.

fields.what: A piece of functionality written in user-focused language, implemented within an iteration, representing a small vertical slice of system behaviour.
fields.pollux: One view, one filter, one export — each a slice a fortnight can carry.

fields.what: Stories give just enough information for business and technical people to understand the intent; details are deferred until implementation.
fields.pollux: Detail on maturity buckets waits until the story is pulled.

fields.what: Through acceptance criteria and acceptance tests, stories become more specific, helping to ensure system quality.
fields.pollux: Nobody argues with Curie's acceptance criteria.

fields.what: The main consumer is the Agile Project Core Team, though the Business Manager and User Representatives in the BIG also use them.
fields.pollux: Hopper reads the same stories the team implements.

fields.what: Non-business effort enabling the features: architecture, infrastructure, evaluating options, legal compliance, continuous improvement and non-functional requirements.
fields.pollux: Data-protection work for national-authority access is enablement, not a feature.

fields.what: Enabler items must always be visible and considered when prioritising; the ArOw helps the PrOw find the right balance.
fields.pollux: Conflict 5 — all-enabler stalls value; all-business collapses velocity later.

traps: The guide never uses the word 'epic' — features decompose directly into stories.
Features are functional units, stories are work units — not the other way round.
A feature rarely fits one iteration; a story must fit one.
Enabler stories are requirements too and compete for Work Items List priority.
Feature prioritisation involves the BM, Project Owner and BIG, not only the PrOw.
